cells.tense: Right now the hand that decides is steady and what gets kept is staying kept.
cells.ask: Pick one thing in your care that has finished its work and let it end this week, then start the one you've been circling.
cells.core:
You are the one who decides what stays and what goes. Nobody handed you that job, and you're not guessing at it either — you know what has finished its work and what still holds. What you keep stays kept, and people around you can feel that it does.

When it's like this, the release isn't loud. Something reaches its end, and what it leaves behind turns into material for the next thing. That's what you're steady at right now: telling the difference between a thing that's done and a thing being abandoned. What keeps this honest is letting the ending happen at the speed the thing actually moves, no faster.
cells.sheetLine: You know what's finished, and you let it finish.
cells.verb: releasing what's used up and turning it into ground for what grows next
cells.place: at the point where direction is decided and kept to

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead there's a settled version of this, and you're already living in it before it exists.
cells.ask: Put one thing you're holding back into use this week, imperfect as it is, and let the using show you what still needs work.
cells.core:
You're standing in the after. Before anyone asked, before the next thing is even ready, you've cleared space for it and replaced what's still working fine. From the inside it looks like foresight, like care. From the outside, people keep finding furniture moved when they weren't looking.

The one who stewards can also be the one who takes things away too early. What would steady this isn't a better plan. It's letting something stay in place until the people using it say it's finished. What you're good at — seeing the end coming — turns into pressure when it gets ahead of the people still in the middle of using the thing.
cells.sheetLine: You're clearing space before anyone asked you to.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you, waiting for a room on the other side.
cells.ask: Do one small thing with your hands on something you've been circling — water it, open it, use a little of it — then stop for today.
cells.core:
There's a box you haven't opened, or a room you haven't entered, or a number you haven't looked at. What you keep still gets kept — the surfaces stay clean — but nothing changes hands anymore. You are not lazy. Something got heavy, and the hand that decides went quiet, and staying quiet has been easier than finding out.

What the whole thing was for hasn't moved. It's just not being touched. What helps next is small and physical: one object, one action, then done. Not a plan. Not a feeling about the plan. A hand on the thing itself, for a few minutes, and a real stop.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping things without touching them.

cells.tense: You're the one running this, and you've been saying it runs itself.
cells.ask: Without announcing it, fix one thing that keeps going wrong — move it once, set where it goes — then say nothing about it.
cells.core:
Look at what holds around you — the repairs, the schedules, the things replaced before they break. Something keeps those going, and it isn't the calendar and it isn't luck. It does the same work in the same place, carefully, and calls itself nothing.

What you keep looks like it happens on its own. That's the part that isn't yours yet — not the doing, the owning. You are already the one who decides what stays and what goes; the only thing missing is your own word on it, said quietly, to yourself. Nothing about the work changes when you put your name on it. The next time someone needs it, you'd be a little less surprised that it was you.
cells.sheetLine: You've been keeping all of it. You call it nothing.

attempts.check: The record does not say what the person actually controls at home or work; a reader could reasonably say the resources are joint or someone else's, and the call is only mine to make about my own attention and budget. The asks survive a wrong read because each is doable with one object, one list, or one sentence and still teaches something about timing. The sentence that serves me more than them: any line implying they should feel grateful for being seen through — cut. The sentence that serves them: none of the four cores says what follows after the act; each stays with the act or its moment, and the Too Little ask will not carry if they read it as another demand from an empty tank.
